question: The Supreme Court of Cassation in Rome ruled on 19 January 2024 that a fascist salute is not considered illegal unless it endangers public order or promotes the resurgence of fascist ideologies. This ruling comes days after hundreds of neo-fascists demonstrated their support for the fascist ideology with a fascist salute in Rome at the beginning of January at a non-related gathering.

Such frequent extremist rallies, not just in Italy but also across Europe, should shake everyone to their very core and should worry the EU institutions. Fascism inflicted unimaginable suffering upon millions of Europeans.

The European Union, in stark contrast, was established upon the foundational principle of anti-fascism, embracing core values such as respect for human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law, and the safeguarding of human rights – values that fascist and Nazi ideologies sought to dismantle. 1.
Does the Commission consider fascist salutes in any shape or form a direct threat to the core European values as enshrined in Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union?
Are such displays of fascist ideology in line with EU law?
Does the Commission intend to take concrete measures to protect the EU from such threats?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.5.2024) The Commission condemns any form of violence and hatred, including manifestations of racism, antisemitism, xenophobia, and other forms of intolerance which are incompatible with the EU values.

The Framework Decision on combating racism and xenophobia1 obliges Member States to criminalise hate speech (public incitement to violence or hatred directed against a group of persons or a member of such a group defined by reference to race, colour, religion, descent or national or ethnic origin).

It also requires the criminalisation of the denial, condoning and gross trivialisation of international crimes, including the Holocaust. It is for the national authorities to establish whether the national criminal law provisions implementing the Framework Decision apply in specific circumstances, taking into account the context and the situation of each case.

To combat racism and antisemitism, the Commission presented in September 2020 the EU anti-racism action plan2 and, in October 2021, the EU Strategy on combating antisemitism and fostering Jewish life3 and is currently implementing a range of actions.

In December 2023, the Commission and the High Representative adopted a Joint Communication on ‘No place for hate: a Europe united against hatred’4 aimed at stepping up EU efforts to fight hatred in all its forms. Through the Radicalisation Awareness Network5, the Commission supports first-line practitioners and policymakers in their fight against radicalisation.
